Sandbox resource management and foreground deletion

44.summary: Practical guide to configuring SAP BTP destinations for six common service types: S/4HANA Cloud (OAuth2ClientCredentials), S/4HANA On-Premise (via Cloud Connector), SAP Integration Suite/CPI (OAuth2 to iFlow endpoints), SAP SaaS (SuccessFactors, Ariba, Concur), external REST APIs, and principal propagation (user identity forwarding). Emphasizes that destination configuration depends on proxy type (Internet vs OnPremise), authentication model of target service, and connectivity path.
key_points: Proxy type selection is foundational: Internet (direct/cloud) vs OnPremise (via Cloud Connector)
S/4HANA Cloud requires OAuth 2.0 with client credentials and token endpoint from cloud system
On-premise requires two-layer configuration: destination (virtual host from Cloud Connector) AND Cloud Connector mapping
Integration Suite endpoints authenticate the same way as target iFlow configuration
SaaS services vary—must first understand target service's authentication model before creating destination
Principal propagation requires end-to-end trust configuration across BTP, Cloud Connector, and backend
technical_details: S/4HANA Cloud: OAuth2ClientCredentials with client credentials and token endpoint
S/4HANA On-Premise: Cloud Connector with virtual host mapping and local authentication
SAP Integration Suite/CPI: iFlow endpoints with OAuth2
SAP SaaS (SuccessFactors, Ariba, Concur): service-specific authentication
External REST APIs: OAuth2, Basic Auth, certificate-based authentication
Proxy Type selection: Internet vs OnPremise
Principal Propagation for user identity forwarding

44.developer_problem: Selecting correct destination configuration (proxy type, authentication, URL format) for different backend systems to establish secure BTP-to-backend connectivity.
44.teaching_angle: Good for teaching BTP connectivity patterns, Cloud Connector role, OAuth2 delegation, and the distinction between technical (destination) and platform-level (Cloud Connector, IAM) configuration. Shows why connectivity requires holistic thinking across layers.

81.summary: This blog explains how to configure SAP BTP Agentic AI to run as unattended scheduled jobs via the Job Scheduling Service, replacing chat-triggered execution. The author covers the 'Expose as an API-triggered job' switch, which unlocks API slug, run prompt, timeout, and service account identity configuration. Two endpoints (POST /api/agents/{slug}/run and POST /api/workflows/{slug}/run) return 202 Accepted and run in background tasks. Authentication is handled by storing oauth2 credentials per user and designating a service account principal for unattended execution; the scheduler passes x-sap-job-id, x-sap-job-schedule-id, x-sap-job-run-id headers.
key_points: Agents execute as background jobs via two POST endpoints that return 202 Accepted; eliminates manual prompting for recurring tasks
Service account identity configured via 'Run as principal' field using stored oauth2 tokens; critical for unattended execution at 03:00 with no logged-in user
xs-security.json scope protection: '$XSAPPNAME.JOBSCHEDULER' with 'grant-as-authority-to-apps' directive to allow Job Scheduling Service direct calls
Job schedules stored in service instance, not mta.yaml; schedules persist across redeployments unlike IaC-driven configuration
Credential status panel shows per-toolset authorization state; nightly token refresh scheduled to prevent refresh token expiry between runs
Output validation via Pydantic AI structured type; enforces one-sentence summary and body_md markdown format with Mermaid rendering, HTML stripping
technical_details: mta.yaml ordering: declare jobscheduler resource before uaa-service; set enable-parallel-deployments: false
Job Scheduling Service cron: seven-field format (custom format, not standard)
Pacemaker monitoring headers: x-sap-job-id, x-sap-job-schedule-id, x-sap-job-run-id
Async execution timeout: 1800 seconds (app returns 202 without calling Update Run Log callback)
OAuth2 credential storage: per user, service account authorizes toolsets via browser once
Preflight checks: distinguish 'no principal configured' from 'principal with stale credential'
81.why_it_matters: Demonstrates BTP's enterprise automation capability for unattended operations without human intervention; relevant for building monitoring, reporting, and system health check workflows that execute outside business hours. Shows identity/auth delegation pattern for service accounts.
81.teaching_angle: Interview prep: 'How would you authenticate an agent running unattended at 3 AM with no logged-in user?' Class exercise: Build a scheduled HANA health check agent, configure service account principal, verify token refresh lifecycle. Demonstrates BTP security patterns (scope delegation) and async job pattern for 15-second API timeout limits.

Read operations succeed (HTTP 200 for service root, $metadata, value helps); POST fails with 403
CSRF token IS present in POST request headers but rejected anyway—not a missing token issue
ARBE cookie absent from requests; BAS session cookie present
OData model configured useBatch: false; batching not the cause
Issue reproducible, affects Fiori Elements List Report/Object Page pattern

51.summary: Production S/4HANA experienced eight HA cluster failovers over three months, all during Monday early morning (UTC). Root cause: Linux fstrim utility scheduled weekly to run during that window; I/O pressure caused Pacemaker monitoring commands (hdbnsutil, Python scripts) to exceed 60-second timeout, triggering cluster to demote primary and initiate failover. Author provides detailed investigation timeline, strace analysis showing chmod operations blocked during fstrim, and resolution (systemctl disable fstrim.timer). No failovers after disabling.
key_points: fstrim.timer: systemd timer enabled by default on SLES, runs Monday UTC midnight-1:00 AM; 27-30 min on production vs. 2 min on non-prod
Failover mechanism: fstrim I/O pressure → hdbnsutil/Python timeout (60s) → Pacemaker retries → multiple timeouts → cluster interprets node unresponsive → demotion/failover
Investigation pattern: All eight failovers in same UTC Monday window; antivirus eliminated; fstrim correlation discovered via systemd timer review
strace evidence: chmod operations on trace files blocked for extended duration during fstrim window; normal ~milliseconds, fstrim window ~seconds
Pacemaker SAPHanaTopology resource agent: 60s timeout per monitor; multiple consecutive timeouts trigger failover
Resolution: 100% effective; no failovers after disabling timer; demonstrated via isolation test (antivirus disabled alone did not resolve)
technical_details: Infrastructure: SAP S/4HANA scale-out on SAP HANA, SLES Pacemaker HA cluster
Monitoring tools: hdbnsutil, Python scripts, strace
Storage: XFS filesystem on NVMe via device-mapper (dm)
Failover timeline events: Last successful monitor (~6s) → degraded (T+10s) → timeout loop (T+10s to T+6min) → demotion (T+6min) → failover (T+~13min total)
Resolution commands: systemctl stop fstrim.timer; systemctl disable fstrim.timer
51.why_it_matters: HA cluster failovers cause complete business outages; identifying hidden system utilities that interfere with database/cluster is critical for production stability. Demonstrates investigation methodology: pattern recognition → hypothesis → isolation testing → strace verification.
51.teaching_angle: Root cause analysis: Use timing patterns as diagnostic clue; isolate variables systematically (antivirus vs. fstrim); validate with strace before/after. Infrastructure understanding: How I/O subsystem impacts database operations and cluster health. Interview: 'Production failover every Monday morning. Walk me through investigation steps and explain why fstrim matters.'

digest.headline: Thin day for core ABAP: CONVERT_CURRENCY in SQLScript, Word generation from ABAP Cloud, two CSRF 403 threads, and MCP/agent tooling around RFC and BTP.
digest.overview:
Today's material has little ABAP-specific news. The useful technical items are a guide to CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SQLScript (HANA XSA, HANA Cloud, Datasphere) [10], and a method for generating .docx files from ABAP Cloud on S/4HANA Public Edition using Word Content Controls bound to a Custom XML Part [14]. The Q&A threads show OData V2 problems: HTTP 403 CSRF failures in BAS Preview [28] and on a QRE system [30], and lost child rows in a Fiori $batch changeset [76].

The rest is AI and platform material. It covers pyrfc-mcp, a policy-controlled MCP bridge to RFC function modules [5], scheduled agents on BTP [81], and the SAP/NVIDIA OpenShell announcement [43]. There is also an infrastructure root-cause write-up in which fstrim caused HANA HA failovers [51]. For ABAP trainers, the value is in the currency, document-generation and OData debugging topics. The AI items are context only. Several items (55, 59, 7) had no usable body text.

deep_dives.title: CONVERT_CURRENCY() in SQLScript and the HDI synonym pattern
deep_dives.explanation:
`CONVERT_CURRENCY()` is a built-in SQLScript function. Use it instead of joining `TCURR` yourself and reimplementing rate selection. The parameters are `AMOUNT`, `SOURCE_UNIT`, `TARGET_UNIT`, `REFERENCE_DATE`, `CLIENT`, `SCHEMA`, `CONVERSION_TYPE` and `ERROR_HANDLING` [10].

`CONVERSION_TYPE` (M/P/B) controls how the exchange rate is selected. The function reads the currency customizing tables (`TCURR`, `TCURF`, and related tables). In an HDI container you cannot read those tables directly. You reach them through synonyms such as `TCURR_CV_SYN` and `TCURF_CV_SYN`. That is the main setup step in XSA, HANA Cloud and Datasphere [10].

Unit-of-measure normalization is a separate step, using the `UMREZ`/`UMREN` factors. A pricing model can therefore normalize both currency and unit in one pipeline. For ABAP developers, the same function fits AMDP methods on HANA. In CDS you would normally use the `currency_conversion` function instead. This is my inference; the source covers SQLScript only.

deep_dives.title: Word documents from ABAP Cloud with Content Controls and Custom XML
deep_dives.explanation:
The usual approach to .docx output is to build or patch OOXML in ABAP, which is fragile. This method reverses it. The template is a normal Word file whose Content Controls are bound to a Custom XML Part. At runtime ABAP builds the data XML and swaps exactly one file inside the ZIP container. Word does the rendering when the document is opened [14].

Because only one part changes, the risk of corrupting the package is small. The approach uses only released APIs on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. That matters under ABAP Cloud rules, where you cannot rely on unreleased ZIP or XML utilities. A repository app lets business users upload and manage templates without a developer.

The author lists specific OOXML pitfalls and says the approach does not work for Excel [14]. The excerpt does not give the code. To teach it, you would reproduce the ZIP replacement yourself, using `cl_abap_zip` if it is released in your system (verify in ADT).
key_concepts: Replacing one file in the OOXML ZIP

deep_dives.title: Diagnosing OData V2 CSRF 403 and lost $batch child rows
deep_dives.explanation:
Two threads report 403 'CSRF token validation failed' although the token is sent. In BAS Preview, GET requests work and the POST fails. The response header `X-CSRF-Token: Required` is returned, the `useBatch: false` model setting is in use, and the same app works when deployed [28]. On the QRE system, several existing services began failing on `$batch` POSTs on 28 Sept, while the token fetch succeeds [30]. Neither thread gives a root cause.

A practical order of checks: confirm the token is fetched from the same host and session that later sends the POST (the ARBE cookie is missing in [28]). Compare the fetch and POST request headers. Check for a proxy or a session change between the two calls. Then check the Gateway side (SM59, /IWFND/ERROR_LOG, ICF/session settings) and any recent transports or kernel changes. These are suggestions, not findings from the threads.

The F2551 thread is a different problem: 'Scoring is not a deferred group' during `submitChanges` means the child entity was not in a deferred batch group, so the rows were left out of the changeset. A related `LOAD_PROGRAM_INTF_MISMATCH` dump in `IF_MDQ_DS_TYPES` had been fixed earlier [76]. Compare the console warning, the `$batch` payload and ST22 together.

interview_questions.question: You need multi-currency conversion in a HANA-side SQLScript model. How do you do it, and what changes inside an HDI container?
interview_questions.answer: Use the built-in `CONVERT_CURRENCY()` function and don't write your own exchange-rate join. Its parameters are AMOUNT, SOURCE_UNIT, TARGET_UNIT, REFERENCE_DATE, CLIENT, SCHEMA, CONVERSION_TYPE and ERROR_HANDLING. CONVERSION_TYPE (M/P/B) controls how the rate is chosen. Inside an HDI container you cannot read the TCUR* tables directly, so you access them through synonyms such as TCURR_CV_SYN and TCURF_CV_SYN. Unit-of-measure normalization is a separate step using UMREZ/UMREN factors. Central conversion keeps results consistent with SAP's own exchange-rate framework and avoids duplicated logic.

interview_questions.question: An OData V2 POST returns 403 'CSRF token validation failed' although the request carries a token. How do you investigate?
interview_questions.answer: First establish scope. In the BAS Preview case only the POST failed and GET worked, and the deployed app worked [28]. In the QRE case many services failed at once from a specific date [30]. Compare the token fetch with the POST: same host, same session cookies, and the same token value. A missing session cookie or a proxy in between can make the server reject a token it issued. Check for changes on the Gateway side, such as configuration, transports or kernel, using /IWFND/ERROR_LOG. Test the same call outside the browser to separate a client problem from a server problem. Do not conclude 'known defect' without evidence, because neither thread has a confirmed cause.

interview_questions.question: How would you expose RFC-enabled function modules to an AI agent safely?
interview_questions.answer: Do not give the agent open RFC access. The pyrfc-mcp pattern places a policy-controlled layer between the agent and SAP [5]. It restricts which function modules can be discovered and called, handles transactions explicitly, limits response size, and writes an audit log of each call. On the ABAP side, use a dedicated technical user with a minimal authorization profile (S_RFC and the application authorization objects). That user is the real boundary, because the MCP layer only adds control. Prefer read-only or wrapper function modules, so the agent never calls a BAPI that commits changes directly. Test with the synthetic demo mode before connecting a real system.
